claims.source: We also noted that PCGF6 target genes harbor CGIs that tend to be slightly shorter and more methylated than CBX7 targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: PCGF6 targets are bound by KDM2B.
claims.source: Consistently, PCGF6 targets were bound by KDM2B.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claims.claim: KDM2B loss induces a subtle increase of RING1B binding at PCGF6 targets.
claims.source: KDM2B loss induced a subtle increase of RING1B binding at PCGF6 targets while RING1B binding at CBX7 targets was marginally decreased (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: PCGF6-bound genes are up-regulated to a much lesser extent than CBX7-bound genes in Kdm2b-KO ESCs.
claims.source: Moreover, PCGF6-bound genes were up-regulated to a much lesser extent than CBX7-bound genes in Kdm2b-KO ESCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: CGI recognition by KDM2B has distinct roles for PCGF6-PRC1 recruitment from that reported for cPRC1.
claims.source: These results suggest that the CGI recognition by KDM2B has distinct roles for PCGF6-PRC1 recruitment from that reported for cPRC1 (Farcas et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the data showing different effects of KDM2B loss on PCGF6 vs CBX7 targets (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G) compared to the cited literature.

claims.claim: More than 250 genes are considerably up-regulated in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: To test this, we performed RNA-seq and found that more than 250 genes were considerably up-regulated in Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Genes up-regulated in Pcgf6-KO ESCs are a subset of genes up-regulated in Ring1A/B-dKO ESCs.
claims.source: Importantly, these genes were a subset of the genes up-regulated in the Ring1A and Ring1B double knockout (Ring1A/B-dKO) ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: PCGF6+RING1B+ genes are barely transcribed in WT ESCs.
claims.source: This analysis showed that the PCGF6+RING1B+ genes were barely transcribed in WT ESCs; likewise, the PCGF6-RING1B+ genes were marginally expressed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the FPKM analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: PCGF6+RING1B- genes that harbor CGIs are robustly expressed in WT ESCs.
claims.source: In contrast, the PCGF6+RING1B- group that harbors CGIs was robustly expressed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the FPKM analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Both PCGF6+RING1B+ and PCGF6-RING1B+ genes are significantly up-regulated in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: We found both PCGF6+RING1B+ and PCGF6-RING1B+ genes were significantly up-regulated while expression levels of PCGF6+RING1B- or PCGF6-RING1B- genes were barely altered in Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 2A, left).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Expression levels of PCGF6+RING1B- or PCGF6-RING1B- genes are barely altered in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: We found both PCGF6+RING1B+ and PCGF6-RING1B+ genes were significantly up-regulated while expression levels of PCGF6+RING1B- or PCGF6-RING1B- genes were barely altered in Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 2A, left).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Expression levels of highly up-regulated genes in the PCGF6+RING1B+ category are considerably higher than those in the PCGF6-RING1B+ category in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: We however also found that expression levels of highly up-regulated genes (more than 5-times; indicated by red lines in Figure 2A) in the PCGF6+RING1B+ category were considerably higher than those in the PCGF6-RING1B+ category in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: PCGF6+RING1B+ and PCGF6-RING1B+ categories are also up-regulated in Ring1A/B-dKO ESCs.
claims.source: Those categories were also up-regulated in Ring1A/B-dKO ESCs (Figure 2A, right), suggesting a functional link between PCGF6 and RING1A/B for down-regulation of such genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the dot plot analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: PCGF6 contributes to RING1B-mediated repression of target genes primarily in the PCGF6+RING1B+ category.
claims.source: Together, PCGF6 is suggested to contribute to RING1B-mediated repression of target genes primarily in the PCGF6+RING1B+ category but also in RING1B targets not bound by PCGF6 to a lesser extent.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the gene expression data in Figure 2A and RT-qPCR validation in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are enriched in meiosis- and germ cell-related genes.
claims.source: To gain insight into the physiological role of PCGF6-PRC1-mediated gene regulation in ESCs, we performed gene ontology (GO) analyses, which revealed that PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are enriched in meiosis- and germ cell-related genes as suggested previously (Zdzieblo et al., 2014), unlike the cPRC1 target genes that are predominantly enriched in developmental genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: cPRC1 target genes are predominantly enriched in developmental genes.
claims.source: To gain insight into the physiological role of PCGF6-PRC1-mediated gene regulation in ESCs, we performed gene ontology (GO) analyses, which revealed that PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are enriched in meiosis- and germ cell-related genes as suggested previously (Zdzieblo et al., 2014), unlike the cPRC1 target genes that are predominantly enriched in developmental genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1 has a potential role for suppression of the meiotic program or germ cell differentiation program in ESCs.
claims.source: These results suggest a potential role of PCGF6-PRC1 for suppression of the meiotic program or germ cell differentiation program, or both, in ESCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the GO analysis showing enrichment of meiosis and germ cell genes among PCGF6 targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: H2AK119ub1 is considerably enriched at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes.
claims.source: Indeed, ChIP-qPCR analyses revealed considerable enrichment of H2AK119ub1 at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: H2AK119ub1 enrichment at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes is dramatically diminished in the absence of Pcgf6.
claims.source: Furthermore, this H2AK119ub1 enrichment was dramatically diminished in the absence of Pcgf6, revealing a role for PCGF6 in mediating H2AK119ub1 deposition (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: H2AK119ub1 enrichment at cPRC1 targets (Zic1 and Hoxd11) is marginally affected in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: In contrast, H2AK119ub1 enrichment at Zic1 and Hoxd11, cPRC1 targets, was marginally affected in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, further supporting our model that PCGF6 is not primarily involved in cPRC1-dependent repression (Figure 2C, middle).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Mutations of RING1B residue I53 (I53S or I53A) abrogate its E3 ligase activity by disrupting interactions with UBCH5C.
claims.source: Previous reports have demonstrated that mutations of RING1B residue I53 (i.e., I53S or I53A), abrogated its E3 ligase activity by disrupting its interactions with the E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UBCH5C (also known as UBE2D3: Ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme E2 D3) (Ben-Saadon et al., 2006; Buchwald et al., 2006; Endoh et al., 2012; Eskeland et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: Rescuing Ring1A/B-dKO cells with I53 mutants fails to maintain transcriptional repression of PCGF6 target genes.
claims.source: Rescuing the Ring1A/B-dKO cells with the I53 mutants failed to maintain transcriptional repression, demonstrating that repression of PCGF6 target genes depends on the catalytic activity of RING1B and likely also downstream H2AK119ub1 deposition (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Repression of PCGF6 target genes depends on the catalytic activity of RING1B and downstream H2AK119ub1 deposition.
claims.source: Rescuing the Ring1A/B-dKO cells with the I53 mutants failed to maintain transcriptional repression, demonstrating that repression of PCGF6 target genes depends on the catalytic activity of RING1B and likely also downstream H2AK119ub1 deposition (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data showing that catalytically inactive RING1B mutants cannot rescue repression (Figure 2D).

claims.claim: H2AK119ub1 plays a critical role for recruitment of PRC2 and downstream H3K27me3 deposition.
claims.source: Since our previous report demonstrated that H2AK119ub1 plays a critical role for recruitment of PRC2 and downstream H3K27me3 deposition (Blackledge et al., 2014), we thus investigated H3K27me3 deposition at the representative PCGF6 bound genes, and indeed found a significant H3K27me3 enrichment at these targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work and ChIP-qPCR data in this study (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claims.claim: H3K27me3 deposition at PCGF6-PRC1 targets is mediated by the PRC2 complex.
claims.source: As expected, the H3K27me3 level was markedly reduced in the absence of the key PRC2 component EED (embryonic ectoderm development), confirming that H3K27me3 deposition in these genes is mediated by the PRC2 complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing loss of H3K27me3 in Eed-KO ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).

claims.claim: H3K27me3 level at PCGF6-PRC1 targets is considerably reduced in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: We indeed found a considerable reduction in H3K27me3 level at these PCGF6-PRC1 targets in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, but only marginally at cPRC1 targets, suggesting a potential role for PCGF6-mediated H2AK119ub1 to recruit PRC2 (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: PRC2-mediated mechanisms exhibit only limited impact on the repression of PCGF6-PRC1 targets.
claims.source: However, consistent with a previous report (Riising et al., 2014), PRC2-mediated mechanisms exhibited only limited impact on the repression of PCGF6-PRC1 targets (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression data in Eed-KO ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) and a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: PCGF6 physically interacts with RING1B through its RING finger domain.
claims.source: Previous studies have reported that PCGF6 interacts with RING1B through its RING finger domain (Akasaka et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Ectopic targeting of PCGF6/TETR fusion protein to a TetO array leads to sequential binding of RING1B, H2AK119ub1 deposition and PRC2 recruitment.
claims.source: ChIP-qPCR analysis showed binding of the PCGF6/TETR fusion protein at the TetO array. Importantly, this was accompanied by considerable enrichment of RING1B, MAX and H2AK119ub1, indicating that PCGF6 recruits PCGF6-PRC1 (Figure 3A). We also observed association of EZH2 and H3K27me3 with the TetO array, likely mediated by the upstream H2AK119ub1 as reported previously (Blackledge et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data from the tethering experiment shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: RING1B binding to PCGF6-PRC1 target genes is considerably depleted in the absence of Pcgf6.
claims.source: This experiment demonstrated that RING1B binding to PCGF6-PRC1 target genes such as Tex19.1, Tdrkh, Syce1 (synaptonemal complex central element protein 1) and Mael (maelstrom spermatogenic transposon silencer) was indeed considerably depleted in the absence of Pcgf6 (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: RING1B binding to cPRC1 target sites, such as the Hoxb cluster, is unaffected in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: In contrast, RING1B binding to cPRC1 target sites, such as the Hoxb cluster, was unaffected.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: RING1B binding to core PCGF6-PRC1 target genes (PCGF6+CBX7-RING1B+) is considerably reduced in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: We observed considerable reduction of RING1B binding to the core PCGF6-PRC1 target genes (PCGF6+CBX7-RING1B+) in Pcgf6-KO (green dot plots in Figure 3C, left; green lines in Figure 3C, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: cPRC1 target genes (PCGF6-CBX7+RING1B+) are not affected by Pcgf6 deletion.
claims.source: In contrast, cPRC1 target genes (PCGF6-CBX7+RING1B+) were not affected.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Genetic ablation of Pcgf2 (Mel18) and Pcgf4 (Bmi1) leads to reduction of RING1B binding only at cPRC1 target genes.
claims.source: Consistent with these observations, genetic ablation of Pcgf2 (Mel18) and Pcgf4 (Bmi1), both of which are essential components of the cPRC1 complex, led to reduction of RING1B binding of only cPRC1 target genes (PCGF6-CBX7+RING1B+) (blue dot plots in Figure 3C, left; blue lines in Figure 3C, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: PCGF6 preferentially recruits RING1B to PCGF6-PRC1 targets, but not to cPRC1 targets.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings indicate that PCGF6 preferentially recruits RING1B to PCGF6-PRC1 targets, but not to cPRC1 targets.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing differential effects of Pcgf6 deletion on RING1B binding at different target classes (Figure 3B,C).

claims.claim: PCGF6 H155Y mutant fails to interact with RING1B while retaining the ability to associate with L3MBTL2 and MAX.
claims.source: We expressed the mutant in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, and noted that it indeed failed to interact with RING1B, while retaining the ability to associate with L3MBTL2 and MAX (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: PCGF6 H155Y mutant can bind target genes but fails to recruit RING1B.
claims.source: ChIP-qPCR analysis showed that although the mutant PCGF6 could bind the indicated target genes, it failed to recruit RING1B (Figure 3D) and, as a result, H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 marks were also not established in the target genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: PCGF6 H155Y mutant fails to repress PCGF6-PRC1 target genes.
claims.source: Consistent with this interpretation, the mutant PCGF6 failed to repress PCGF6-PRC1 targets genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: PCGF6 contributes to the assembly and recruitment of the PCGF6-PRC1 complex by direct physical interactions with RING1B.
claims.source: Based on these observations, we concluded that PCGF6 contributes to the assembly and recruitment of the PCGF6-PRC1 complex by direct physical interactions with RING1B, which likely plays a critical role to mediate the repression.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutant analysis showing that disrupting PCGF6-RING1B interaction abolishes repression (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

claims.claim: PCGF6 is dispensable for L3MBTL2 binding to gene promoters.
claims.source: Indeed, we noted that PCGF6 was dispensable for L3MBTL2 binding of gene promoters (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 may function in parallel to recruit ncPRC1 complexes.
claims.source: As L3MBTL2 has been reported as a recruiter of ncPRC1 (Qin et al., 2012; Trojer et al., 2011), this observation suggests that PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 may function in parallel to recruit ncPRC1 complexes.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that L3MBTL2 binding is independent of PCGF6 (Figure 3E) combined with cited literature on L3MBTL2 function.

claims.claim: H3K9me2 levels at PCGF6-PRC1 targets do not show considerable changes in Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: We went on to examine contribution of H3K9me2, which is mediated by G9A/GLP, for PCGF6-PRC1-target repression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D). Unlike L3mbtl2-KO ESCs (Qin et al., 2012), we did not observe considerable changes in H3K9me2 levels in Pcgf6-KO.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the heat map analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The L3MBTL2/G9A axis is marginally involved in PCGF6-mediated repression.
claims.source: Together, we suggest that the L3MBTL2/G9A axis is marginally involved in PCGF6-mediated repression.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of H3K9me2 changes in Pcgf6-KO (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: CBX1/3 have a marginal role for the repression of PCGF6-PRC1 targets in ESCs.
claims.source: We did not observe a significant change in the expression levels of PCGF6+CBX7-RING1B+ in Cbx1/3-dKO ESCs, suggesting that CBX1/3 have, if any, a marginal role for the repression of PCGF6-PRC1 targets in ESCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by gene expression analysis in Cbx1/3-dKO ESCs shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: H3K27me3 is dispensable for locus-specific recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1.
claims.source: We did not observe any significant differences in FLAG-PCGF6 binding between WT and Eed-KO cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that H3K27me3 is dispensable for locus-specific recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data comparing PCGF6 binding in WT and Eed-KO ESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).

claims.claim: H2AK119ub1 levels at genes bound by PCGF6 are not affected in Eed-KO ESCs.
claims.source: Consistently, H2AK119ub1 levels at genes bound by PCGF6 were not affected in the Eed-KO (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: PCGF2 barely associates with PCGF6 targets irrespective of H3K27me3 status.
claims.source: In contrast, PCGF2, a component of cPRC1, barely associates with PCGF6 targets irrespective of H3K27me3 status, while it strongly associates with cPRC1 targets such as Zic1 and Hoxb3 in an EED-dependent manner (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The H3K27me3-dependent pathway to recruit cPRC1 is barely active at PCGF6-PRC1 targets.
claims.source: These findings suggests that the H3K27me3-dependent pathway to recruit cPRC1 is barely active at PCGF6-PRC1 targets.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PCGF2 does not bind PCGF6 targets even when H3K27me3 is present (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claims.claim: The E-box motif CACGTG is enriched within PCGF6-bound promoters.
claims.source: We observed enrichment of the E-box motif CACGTG, a DNA sequence that is recognized by the bHLH-containing transcription factors including MAX (Blackwood and Eisenman, 1991), within these promoters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The E-box motif CACGTG is not enriched in RING1B- or CBX7-bound genes.
claims.source: Importantly, this motif was not enriched in RING1B- or CBX7-bound genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the E-box motif is a feature of PCGF6-PRC1 targets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: There is considerable overlap between PCGF6-bound and MAX-bound genes.
claims.source: Consistent with this notion, we observed considerable overlap between PCGF6-bound and MAX-bound genes, while the overlap between PCGF6-bound and MYC-bound genes was much less (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: MGA forms a heterodimer with MAX and binds the CACGTG E-box motif.
claims.source: Interestingly, MGA, a transcription factor that also forms a heterodimer with MAX and binds the CACGTG E-box motif (Hurlin et al., 1999), is included in the PCGF6 complex determined by us (Figure 1B) and others (Gao et al., 2012; Hauri et al., 2016; Kloet et al., 2016; Ogawa et al., 2002; Qin et al., 2012; Trojer et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and mass spectrometry data in this study (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: Genes bound by MAX, PCGF6 and RING1B (MAX+PCGF6+RING1B+) show significant up-regulation in Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs.
claims.source: Interestingly, genes that were bound by MAX, PCGF6 and RING1B (MAX+PCGF6+RING1B+) showed significant up-regulation in Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Genes bound by PCGF6 and RING1B but not MAX (MAX-PCGF6+RING1B+) are barely up-regulated in Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs.
claims.source: In contrast, genes bound by PCGF6 and RING1B, but not MAX (MAX-PCGF6+RING1B+), were barely up-regulated (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Genes bound only by RING1B (MAX-PCGF6-RING1B+) show significant up-regulation in Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we observed significant up-regulation of genes bound only by RING1B (MAX-PCGF6-RING1B+).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: MAX and MGA primarily contribute to the repression of MAX+PCGF6+RING1B+ genes.
claims.source: We thus suggest MAX and MGA primarily contribute to the repression of MAX+PCGF6+RING1B+ genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing differential effects of Max/Mga knockdown on different gene categories (Figure 4B).

claims.claim: Genes bound by PCGF6, RING1B and MAX but not by MYC are significantly enriched in germ cell- and meiosis-related functions.
claims.source: GO analysis revealed that genes bound by PCGF6, RING1B and MAX but not by MYC (PCGF6+RING1B+MAX+MYC-), were significantly enriched in germ cell- and meiosis-related functions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), further supporting our model that PCGF6-PRC1 functions as a dedicated repressor of genes associated with germ cells and meiosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: PCGF6 binding to target loci depends on MAX and MGA.
claims.source: Indeed, ChIP-qPCR in the Max-KD or Mga-KD ESCs revealed that PCGF6 binding to target loci depends on MAX and MGA (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: MAX and MGA bind their targets in mutually dependent manner.
claims.source: Importantly, MAX and MGA bind these targets in mutually dependent manner (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing that knockdown of either Max or Mga reduces binding of both proteins (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: RING1B and RYBP do not bind to PCGF6-PRC1 target loci in Max-KO ESCs.
claims.source: RING1B and RYBP, which form stoichiometric complexes with PCGF6 (Figure 1B), did not bind to PCGF6-PRC1 target loci in the Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Local H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 levels are considerably decreased at PCGF6-PRC1 targets in Max-KO ESCs.
claims.source: Likewise, local H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 levels were considerably decreased, and binding of L3MBTL2, another key regulator of ncPRC1, into PCGF6-PRC1 target genes was also depleted in the Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: L3MBTL2 binding to PCGF6-PRC1 target genes is depleted in Max-KO ESCs.
claims.source: Likewise, local H2AK119ub1 and H3K27me3 levels were considerably decreased, and binding of L3MBTL2, another key regulator of ncPRC1, into PCGF6-PRC1 target genes was also depleted in the Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Enrichment of RING1B, H2AK119ub1, H3K27me3 and RYBP at Zic1 (a cPRC1 target) does not show considerable changes in Max-KO ESCs.
claims.source: In contrast, enrichment of RING1B, H2AK119ub1, H3K27me3 and RYBP at Zic1, a cPRC1 target, did not show considerable changes in the Max-KO ESCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Recruitment of both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 requires MAX.
claims.source: These results suggest that recruitment of both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 requires MAX.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the ChIP-qPCR data showing loss of both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 binding in Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D).

claims.claim: The MAX/MGA heterodimer recruits PCGF6-PRC1 to its targets.
claims.source: Collectively, these findings indicate that the MAX/MGA heterodimer recruits PCGF6-PRC1 to its targets.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including motif enrichment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 binding (Figure 4C), and loss of PCGF6-PRC1 components in Max-KO (Figure 4D).

claims.claim: MAX plays a role in maintaining ESC proliferation and self-renewal ability.
claims.source: A role for MAX in maintaining ESC proliferation and self-renewal ability has been reported in a previous study (Hishida et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: Conditional deletion of Max leads to slower ESC proliferation and cell differentiation.
claims.source: We also observed that conditional deletion of Max (Max-KO) led to slower ESC proliferation and cell differentiation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Rescuing Max-KO cells with exogenous WT MAX restores cell proliferation and blocks spontaneous differentiation.
claims.source: Rescuing the induced Max-KO cells with an exogenous WT MAX restored cell proliferation and blocked spontaneous differentiation, as expected.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Mutant MAX proteins with defects in the basic region of the bHLH domain fail to rescue Max-KO ESC proliferation defects.
claims.source: In contrast, mutant MAX proteins harboring defects in the basic region of the bHLH (basic helix-loop-helix) domain [hereafter referred to as MAX(VD) or MAX(Δb)] (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, left), failed to do so (Figure 5A, right).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: DNA motif recognition by MAX plays a role in maintaining ESCs by recruiting the PCGF6-PRC1 complex.
claims.source: These findings indicate that DNA motif recognition by MAX plays a role in maintaining ESCs, at least partly by recruiting the PCGF6-PRC1 complex.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MAX mutants defective in DNA binding cannot rescue ESC maintenance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) combined with evidence that MAX recruits PCGF6-PRC1 (Figure 4C,D).

claims.claim: Mutant MAX proteins retain the ability to associate with HA-PCGF6, RING1B and L3MBTL2.
claims.source: Mechanistically, co-IP analyses showed that a FLAG-tagged MAX protein physically interacts with HA-PCGF6, RING1B and L3MBTL2. The mutant MAX proteins also retained the ability to associate and form stable complexes with HA-PCGF6, RING1B and L3MBTL2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claims.claim: FLAG-tagged MAX can restore binding of HA-tagged PCGF6 to target loci in Max-KO ESCs.
claims.source: As expected, ChIP-qPCR revealed that the FLAG-tagged MAX could restore binding of the HA-tagged PCGF6 into target loci in Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D), whereas the mutant MAX proteins failed to bind targets and recruit HA-tagged PCGF6.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D.

claims.claim: Mutant MAX proteins fail to bind targets and recruit HA-tagged PCGF6.
claims.source: As expected, ChIP-qPCR revealed that the FLAG-tagged MAX could restore binding of the HA-tagged PCGF6 into target loci in Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D), whereas the mutant MAX proteins failed to bind targets and recruit HA-tagged PCGF6.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D.

claims.claim: The growth rate of Pcgf6-KO ESCs is significantly slower than WT in the presence of 3i and fetal bovine serum.
claims.source: Indeed, the growth rate of Pcgf6-KO ESCs was significantly slower than the WT in the presence of three inhibitors (3i: SU5402 for FGFR, PD184352 for ERK, and CHIR99021 for GSK3) and fetal bovine serum as suggested previously (Zdzieblo et al., 2014) (Figure 5A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claims.claim: The growth of Pcgf6-KO ESCs is further halted under serum-free condition.
claims.source: The growth of Pcgf6-KO ESCs was further halted under serum-free condition (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Pcgf6-KO ESCs maintain an ESC-like morphology.
claims.source: Unlike the Max-KO, however, Pcgf6-KO ESCs maintained an ESC-like morphology.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by phase-contrast microscopy images shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1 has a role in ESC proliferation but may not be essential to maintain ES cell morphology.
claims.source: These findings support the notion that PCGF6-PRC1 has a role in ESC proliferation, but may not be essential to maintain ES cell morphology.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Pcgf6-KO ESCs grow slowly but maintain ESC morphology (Figure 5A,B,D).

claims.claim: Genetic ablation of Pcgf6 at ESC stage induces growth arrest and cell death.
claims.source: Genetic ablation of Pcgf6 at day −5 induced growth arrest and cell death of ESCs (Figure 5D); while ablation of Pcgf6 at day −2 caused significant growth defects in epiLCs (Figure 5E), revealing a stage-specific role of PCGF6 for growth and survival of ESCs and epiLCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Ablation of Pcgf6 at epiLC stage causes significant growth defects.
claims.source: Genetic ablation of Pcgf6 at day −5 induced growth arrest and cell death of ESCs (Figure 5D); while ablation of Pcgf6 at day −2 caused significant growth defects in epiLCs (Figure 5E), revealing a stage-specific role of PCGF6 for growth and survival of ESCs and epiLCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: OHT-treatment at post-epiLC stage does not induce growth arrest or cell death and even accelerates differentiation and proliferation.
claims.source: In contrast, OHT-treatment at day +2 (post-epiLC stage) did not induce growth arrest or cell death and, surprisingly, even accelerated differentiation and proliferation (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by FACS analysis and cell proliferation data shown in Figure 5F.

claims.claim: The same group of genes (PCGF6+RING1B+ category) are de-repressed in ESCs, epiLCs and PGCLCs in the absence of Pcgf6.
claims.source: We observed that the same group of genes (the PCGF6+RING1B+ category in ESCs) were de-repressed in ESCs, epiLCs and PGCLCs in the absence of Pcgf6.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: The extent of derepression of PCGF6 target genes is similar among ESCs, epiLCs and PGCLCs.
claims.source: Furthermore, the extent of derepression of PCGF6 target genes was also similar among these three cell types.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1-mediated gene silencing is essential to maintain ESC and epiLC, but not PGCLC.
claims.source: Thus, these results indicate that the different phenotypic impacts of Pcgf6 ablation in ESCs, epiLCs and PGCLCs are not due to up-regulation of different sets of genes, but rather suggest that PCGF6-PRC1-mediated gene silencing is essential to maintain ESC and epiLC, but not PGCLC.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that similar genes are de-repressed in all three cell types (Figure 5G) but only ESCs and epiLCs show growth defects (Figure 5D,E,F).

claims.claim: PCGF6 plays a role in maintaining pluripotency by suppressing germ cell potential in ESCs.
claims.source: PCGF6, therefore, plays a role in maintaining pluripotency, likely by suppressing germ cell potential in ESCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that PCGF6 represses germ cell genes and is required for ESC maintenance but not PGCLC maintenance (Figure 5).

claims.claim: Pcgf6 is expressed in broad range of tissues and cell types and abundantly in testis, ESCs and pre-implantation embryos.
claims.source: Consistently, Pcgf6 is expressed in broad range of tissues and cell types and even abundantly in testis, ESCs and pre-implantation embryos (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by expression data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claims.claim: Pcgf6-KO mice are viable and fertile.
claims.source: We found that Pcgf6-KO (−/−) mice were viable and fertile, but were not born at the normal Mendelian ratio (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Pcgf6-KO mice are not born at the normal Mendelian ratio.
claims.source: We found that Pcgf6-KO (−/−) mice were viable and fertile, but were not born at the normal Mendelian ratio (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data showing deviation from expected 1:2:1 ratio (Figure 6D).

claims.claim: Lethality among Pcgf6−/− homozygous embryos can be observed as early as the blastocyst stage (3.5 dpc).
claims.source: Lethality among Pcgf6−/− homozygous embryos could be observed as early as the blastocyst stage [3.5 days post coitum (dpc)].
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data at different developmental stages (Figure 6D).

claims.claim: Embryonic death in the Pcgf6−/− line can be continuously detected during post-implantation development.
claims.source: Furthermore, embryonic death in the Pcgf6−/− line could be continuously detected during post-implantation development.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by genotype distribution data at different developmental stages (Figure 6D).

claims.claim: About one third of the surviving Pcgf6−/− embryos at 10.5 dpc exhibit growth retardation.
claims.source: Consistently, we found that about one third of the surviving Pcgf6−/− embryos at 10.5 dpc exhibited growth retardation (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by embryo images shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: No ESC lines could be established from Pcgf6−/− blastocysts.
claims.source: From 73 blastocysts collected, we could establish 22 ESC-like lines. Remarkably, among these 22 lines, not a single one was homozygous Pcgf6−/− (Figure 6F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the ESC derivation data shown in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Pcgf6-deficient ICMs are functionally different from WT ICMs.
claims.source: As ESCs could not be established from Pcgf6−/− lines, we surmised that Pcgf6-deficient ICMs are functionally different from their WT counterparts.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the failure to establish ESC lines from Pcgf6−/− blastocysts (Figure 6F).

claims.claim: PCGF6 has a role in both pre- and peri-implantation development.
claims.source: Collectively, these results reveal a role for PCGF6 in both pre- and peri-implantation development.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the embryonic lethality data (Figure 6D,E) and failure to establish ESC lines (Figure 6F).

claims.claim: Pcgf6−/− mice exhibit morphological alterations of the vertebrae that represent anterior transformations of the axis.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we observed morphological alterations of the vertebrae that represent anterior transformations of the axis in these mice (Figure 6G,H).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal analysis shown in Figure 6G,H.

claims.claim: PCGF6 over-expression induces posterior transformations of the axis.
claims.source: To further confirm the role of PCGF6 for A-P patterning, we then tested the impacts of PCGF6 over-expression and, indeed, observed posterior transformations of the axis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D.

claims.claim: Skeletal alterations in Pcgf6−/− mice are accompanied by aberrant repression of Hoxb6 at the eighth pre-vertebra.
claims.source: We further found that skeletal alterations in Pcgf6−/− mice were accompanied by aberrant repression of Hoxb6 at the eighth pre-vertebra (Figure 6I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6I.

claims.claim: PCGF6 regulates A-P patterning presumably through regulation of Hox genes.
claims.source: These suggest that PCGF6 regulates A-P patterning presumably through regulation of Hox genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of skeletal transformations (Figure 6G,H) and altered Hoxb6 expression (Figure 6I).

claims.claim: Anterior transformations in Pcgf6−/− mice are suppressed by the Pcgf2 mutation.
claims.source: We indeed observed that anterior transformations in Pcgf6−/− mice were suppressed by the Pcgf2 mutation, suggesting mutually counteracting properties of PCGF6 and PCGF2.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal analysis of double mutants shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F.

claims.claim: Pcgf6−/− mice show significant reduction of placental size.
claims.source: In addition to the skeletal phenotypes, we also noted significant reduction of placental size, manifested by hypoplasticity and malformation of the labyrinth layer, in the Pcgf6−/− mice (Figure 6J,K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis and quantification shown in Figure 6J,K.

claims.claim: The number of spongiotrophoblast cells and trophoblast giant cells is dramatically decreased in Pcgf6−/− mice.
claims.source: In particular, the number of spongiotrophoblast cells and trophoblast giant cells (TGCs), identified by expression of Pl1 (placental lactogen-I, also known as Prl3d1) and Tpbpa (trophoblast specific protein alpha), respectively, was dramatically decreased.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6J.

claims.claim: PCGF6 has roles in peri-implantation development, including A-P specification and regulation of placental development.
claims.source: These findings demonstrate further roles of PCGF6 in peri-implantation development, including A-P specification and regulation of placental development.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the skeletal phenotypes (Figure 6G,H,I) and placental defects (Figure 6J,K) observed in Pcgf6−/− mice.

claims.claim: PCGF6 constitutes a non-canonical PRC1 complex that includes the core PRC1 component RING1B.
claims.source: In the present study, we show that PCGF6 constitutes a non-canonical PRC1 complex, PCGF6-PRC1, that includes the core PRC1 component RING1B.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry (Figure 1A,B) and co-IP data (Figure 1C).

claims.claim: PCGF6 physically interacts with RING1B and plays a role in recruitment of RING1B to target genes.
claims.source: PCGF6 physically interacts with RING1B, and plays a role in recruitment of RING1B to target genes, followed by deposition of H2AK119ub1 and transcriptional silencing.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by co-IP data (Figure 1C), ChIP-seq showing RING1B loss in Pcgf6-KO (Figure 3B,C), and mutant analysis (Figure 3D).

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1 recruits PRC2 to target genes.
claims.source: We have previously reported that the PCGF1-associated ncPRC1 (PCGF1-PRC1) recruits PRC2 to target genes (Blackledge et al., 2014). Here, we demonstrate that PCGF6-PRC1 also has a similar role, as ectopic targeting of a PCGF6 protein fused to the Tet repressor (PCGF6/TETR) to a pre-integrated TetO array leads to sequential binding of RING1B, H2AK119ub1 deposition and PRC2 recruitment in cis (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the tethering experiment shown in Figure 3A and cited previous work.

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1-mediated targeting of PRC2 takes place at endogenous genomic loci, particularly at promoters of genes enriched for germ cell-specific and meiosis-specific functions.
claims.source: Like PCGF1-PRC1, PCGF6-PRC1-mediated targeting of PRC2 also takes place in endogenous genomic loci, in particular at promoters of a certain group of genes that are enriched for germ cell-specific and meiosis-specific functions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 1D-G) and GO analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are distinct from those bound by PCGF1-PRC1 and canonical PRC1.
claims.source: However, these genes are distinct from those bound by PCGF1-PRC1 and canonical PRC1, which mainly include developmental genes (Figure 1D–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data comparing PCGF6 targets with CBX7 targets (Figure 1D-G).

claims.claim: Developmental genes are evolutionarily conserved targets of PcG complexes and are characterized by long CpG island promoters that are usually not marked by DNA methylation.
claims.source: Such developmental genes are evolutionarily conserved targets of PcG complexes, and are characterized by long CpG island (CGI) promoters that are usually not marked by DNA methylation (Sharif et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: KDM2B recruits PCGF1-PRC1 to developmental genes by binding unmethylated CGIs.
claims.source: The CXXC domain containing protein KDM2B recruits PCGF1-PRC1 into these loci by binding unmethylated CGIs (Blackledge et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1 target loci have slightly shorter and more DNA methylated CGIs compared to developmental genes.
claims.source: In contrast, PCGF6-PRC1 target loci tend to have slightly shorter and more DNA methylated CGIs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), where KDM2B seems to play distinct roles from PCGF1-PRC1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: H3K27me3 depositions at PCGF6-PRC1 targets are less active to recruit cPRC1.
claims.source: Indeed, H3K27me3 depositions at PCGF6-PRC1 targets are less active to recruit cPRC1 though underlying mechanisms await elucidative (Figure 1G, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing minimal PCGF2 binding at PCGF6 targets (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).

claims.claim: There are at least two major modes of gene silencing by PRC1: one involving PCGF1-PRC1 and cPRC1 silencing developmental genes, and another involving PCGF6-PRC1 silencing germ cell-specific and meiosis-specific genes.
claims.source: Thus, our findings reveal that there are at least two major modes of gene silencing by PRC1; the first involves PCGF1-PRC1 and cPRC1 and silences developmental genes, while the second involves PCGF6-PRC1 and silences germ cell-specific and meiosis-specific genes (see the model in Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the comprehensive analysis of PCGF6-PRC1 targets compared to other PRC1 complexes throughout the study.

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are enriched for the binding motif of the bHLHZ transcription factor MAX.
claims.source: By surveying DNA sequences of the PCGF6-PRC1 target genes, we find that they are enriched for the binding motif of the bHLHZ (basic helix-loop-helix, also containing a leucine zipper) transcription factor MAX (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: MAX forms a heterodimer with MGA.
claims.source: Previous reports showed that MAX forms a heterodimer with MGA, another E-box binding protein (Hurlin et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: MAX and MGA are directly involved in recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1 to target genes.
claims.source: Interestingly, we identified MGA as a PCGF6 interacting factor by mass-spectrometry (Figure 1A,B), indicating that MAX and MGA may be directly involved in recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1 into target genes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 1A,B) and ChIP-qPCR showing MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 recruitment (Figure 4C).

claims.claim: Both MAX and MGA are enriched at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes.
claims.source: Consistent with this hypothesis, both MAX and MGA were enriched at PCGF6-PRC1 target genes (Figures 1G, 4A and C); and depletion of MAX or MGA by siRNA caused a reduction of PCGF6 binding to these loci (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq and ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figures 1G, 4A and C.

claims.claim: The MAX/MGA heterodimer plays a role in recruitment of the ncPRC1 component L3MBTL2.
claims.source: Previous studies show that the MAX/MGA heterodimer also plays a role in recruitment of the ncPRC1 component L3MBTL2 (Suzuki et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: MAX/MGA independently associates with PCGF6 or L3MBTL2.
claims.source: Our results demonstrate that MAX/MGA independently associates with PCGF6 or L3MBTL2, as ablation of PCGF6 does not affect binding of L3MBTL2 (Figures 3E and 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figures 3E and 4D.

claims.claim: MAX/MGA represses target genes through multiple mechanisms that may function in parallel.
claims.source: These findings indicate that MAX/MGA represses target genes through multiple mechanisms that may function in parallel.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that MAX/MGA recruits both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 independently (Figures 3E, 4D).

claims.claim: ESCs deficient for MAX or MGA show a more drastic phenotype than Pcgf6-KO ESCs.
claims.source: Consistent with this notion, ESCs deficient for MAX or MGA show a more drastic phenotype than the Pcgf6-KO ESCs (Figure 6A,B,D) (Hishida et al., 2011; Washkowitz et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of phenotypes shown in Figure 6A,B,D and citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: L3MBTL2 associates with the H3K9me2 methyltransferases G9A and GLP.
claims.source: Interestingly, L3MBTL2 associates with the H3K9me2 methyltransferases G9A and GLP (Ogawa et al., 2002; Qin et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claims.claim: G9A and GLP silence germ cell-specific genes in ESCs.
claims.source: As G9A and GLP silence germ cell-specific genes in ESCs (Maeda et al., 2013), we speculate that L3MBTL2 contributes to transcriptional repression of these genes in association with G9A and GLP; while the same group of genes are silenced by a parallel pathway involving PCGF6 and RING1B (see the model in Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claims.claim: L3MBTL2 contributes to transcriptional repression of germ cell genes in association with G9A and GLP, while the same genes are silenced by a parallel pathway involving PCGF6 and RING1B.
claims.source: As G9A and GLP silence germ cell-specific genes in ESCs (Maeda et al., 2013), we speculate that L3MBTL2 contributes to transcriptional repression of these genes in association with G9A and GLP; while the same group of genes are silenced by a parallel pathway involving PCGF6 and RING1B (see the model in Figure 7B).
claims.evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the cited literature on G9A/GLP function and the data showing independent recruitment of L3MBTL2 and PCGF6 by MAX/MGA.

claims.claim: The existence of several repressive epigenetic mechanisms targeting germ cell-specific genes suggests the importance of preventing aberrant activation of such genes during pre- and peri-implantation embryonic development.
claims.source: The existence of several repressive epigenetic mechanisms that target germ cell-specific genes suggests the importance of preventing aberrant activation of such genes during pre- and peri-implantation embryonic development.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of multiple parallel repressive mechanisms (PCGF6-PRC1 and L3MBTL2/G9A/GLP) targeting the same genes.

claims.claim: Constitutive deletion of Pcgf6 causes impaired development of the placenta, particularly of the spongiotrophoblast layer and trophoblast giant cells.
claims.source: Furthermore, constitutive deletion of Pcgf6 causes impaired development of the placenta, in particular of the spongiotrophoblast layer and trophoblast giant cells (TGCs) (Figure 6J and K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6J and K.

claims.claim: Aberrant phenotypes are observed in the Pcgf6−/− embryo proper, including defects in anterior-posterior axis specification and ectopic expression of developmental genes such as Hoxb6.
claims.source: Such aberrant phenotypes are also observed in the embryo proper, including defects in anterior-posterior (A-P) axis specification and ectopic expression of developmental genes such as Hoxb6 (Figure 6G, H and I).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by skeletal analysis (Figure 6G,H) and in situ hybridization (Figure 6I).

claims.claim: PCGF6 has a previously unappreciated function for repression of germ cell-specific genes in ESCs.
claims.source: Taken together, we demonstrate a previously unappreciated function of the non-canonical PRC1 component PCGF6 for repression of germ cell-specific genes in ESCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the comprehensive analysis of PCGF6 targets and their de-repression in Pcgf6-KO ESCs throughout the study.

claims.claim: Transcriptional silencing of germ cell-specific genes requires the function of RING1B and H2AK119ub1, but not PRC2 and H3K27me3.
claims.source: We further show that transcriptional silencing of such genes requires the function of RING1B and H2AK119ub1, but not PRC2 and H3K27me3.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data showing RING1B-dependent repression (Figure 2D), H2AK119ub1 requirement (Figure 2C), and limited impact of PRC2 loss (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).

claims.claim: PCGF6-bound genes are enriched for short CGIs, frequently marked by methylated DNA.
claims.source: PCGF6-bound genes are enriched for short CGIs, frequently marked by methylated DNA, and are not bound by PCGF1-PRC1.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: PCGF6-bound genes are not bound by PCGF1-PRC1.
claims.source: PCGF6-bound genes are enriched for short CGIs, frequently marked by methylated DNA, and are not bound by PCGF1-PRC1.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the distinct characteristics of PCGF6 targets compared to PCGF1-PRC1 targets (developmental genes with long unmethylated CGIs).

claims.claim: Developmental genes, which are the main targets of PCGF1-PRC1, are not bound by PCGF6-PRC1.
claims.source: Indeed, developmental genes, which are the main targets of PCGF1-PRC1, are not bound by PCGF6-PRC1, revealing distinct functional roles of these two ncPRC1 complexes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing minimal overlap between PCGF6 and CBX7 targets (Figure 1F).

claims.claim: PCGF6-PRC1 is recruited to target sites by the MAX/MGA heterodimer, while PCGF1-PRC1 is recruited by KDM2B.
claims.source: Consistent with this model, PCGF6-PRC1 is recruited to target sites by the MAX/MGA heterodimer, while PCGF1-PRC1 is recruited by the unmethylated CpG binding protein KDM2B (Farcas et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data showing MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 recruitment (Figure 4C) and a citation to previous work on KDM2B-mediated PCGF1-PRC1 recruitment.

claims.claim: This work shows a link between sequence specific DNA binding by the MAX/MGA heterodimer with PRC1-mediated transcriptional silencing of germ cell-specific genes by PCGF6, for regulation of pre- and post-implantation embryonic development.
claims.source: Our work thus shows a link between sequence specific DNA binding by the MAX/MGA heterodimer with PRC1-mediated transcriptional silencing of germ cell-specific genes by PCGF6, for regulation of pre- and post-implantation embryonic development.
claims.evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings of the study, integrating data on MAX/MGA-dependent PCGF6 recruitment (Figure 4), PCGF6-mediated repression of germ cell genes (Figure 2), and developmental phenotypes (Figure 6).

results.result: PCGF6 forms a non-canonical PRC1 complex (PCGF6-PRC1) that includes RING1A/B, MGA, RYBP, L3MBTL2, YAF2, and other factors, but excludes canonical PRC1 components like PCGF2 and PRC2 components like EZH2.
results.evaluation: Mass spectrometry (Figure 1A,B) and co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 1C) demonstrate that PCGF6 associates with RING1A/B, MGA, RYBP, L3MBTL2, and MAX, but not with PCGF1, PCGF2, EZH2, or SET1. The composition is consistent with a non-canonical PRC1 complex and is reproducible across mouse and human cells.

results.result: PCGF6 recruits RING1B to target genes and mediates H2AK119ub1 deposition, specifically at PCGF6-PRC1 targets but not at canonical PRC1 targets.
results.evaluation: ChIP-seq data (Figure 3B,C) show that RING1B binding is substantially reduced at PCGF6 targets in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, while cPRC1 targets remain unaffected. ChIP-qPCR (Figure 2C) confirms loss of H2AK119ub1 at PCGF6 targets upon Pcgf6 deletion. Tethering experiments (Figure 3A) demonstrate that ectopic PCGF6 recruitment leads to RING1B binding and H2AK119ub1 deposition.

results.result: PCGF6-PRC1 target genes are enriched for germ cell- and meiosis-related genes, distinct from the developmental genes targeted by canonical PRC1 and PCGF1-PRC1.
results.evaluation: ChIP-seq data (Figure 1D-G) show PCGF6 binding at germ cell gene promoters like Tex19.1 and Tdrkh, with minimal overlap with CBX7 (canonical PRC1 marker). Gene ontology analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) confirms significant enrichment of meiosis and germ cell terms among PCGF6 targets, contrasting with developmental gene enrichment in cPRC1 targets.

results.result: Conditional ablation of Pcgf6 in ESCs leads to robust de-repression of germ cell-related genes, particularly those co-bound by PCGF6 and RING1B.
results.evaluation: RNA-seq data (Figure 2A) demonstrate significant up-regulation of PCGF6+RING1B+ genes in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, with the most highly up-regulated genes showing expression levels considerably higher than PCGF6-RING1B+ genes. These de-repressed genes are a subset of those up-regulated in Ring1A/B-dKO ESCs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and RT-qPCR validation (Figure 2B) confirms the findings.

results.result: Repression of PCGF6 target genes depends on the catalytic activity of RING1B and H2AK119ub1 deposition.
results.evaluation: RT-qPCR data (Figure 2D) show that catalytically inactive RING1B mutants (I53S, I53A) fail to rescue repression of PCGF6 target genes in Ring1A/B-dKO ESCs, while wild-type RING1B restores repression. This demonstrates that the E3 ligase activity of RING1B is essential for PCGF6-mediated gene silencing.

results.result: The MAX/MGA heterodimer recruits PCGF6-PRC1 to target loci through recognition of E-box motifs (CACGTG) enriched at PCGF6 target promoters.
results.evaluation: Motif enrichment analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) identifies CACGTG E-box motifs specifically at PCGF6 targets. ChIP-qPCR (Figure 4C) demonstrates that PCGF6 binding depends on MAX and MGA, with both factors binding targets in a mutually dependent manner. RNA-seq (Figure 4B) shows that MAX+PCGF6+RING1B+ genes are significantly up-regulated upon Max or Mga knockdown. ChIP-qPCR in Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D) confirms loss of PCGF6, RING1B, and associated histone marks.

results.result: PCGF6 recruits RING1B through direct physical interaction via its RING finger domain, as demonstrated by a separation-of-function mutant (H155Y).
results.evaluation: Co-IP data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) show that the PCGF6 H155Y mutant fails to interact with RING1B while retaining binding to L3MBTL2 and MAX. ChIP-qPCR (Figure 3D) demonstrates that this mutant can bind target genes but fails to recruit RING1B, H2AK119ub1, or H3K27me3. RT-qPCR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) confirms that the mutant cannot rescue repression of PCGF6 target genes.

results.result: Loss of Pcgf6 impairs ESC and epiLC proliferation and viability while maintaining ESC morphology, indicating a role in cell growth but not morphological maintenance.
results.evaluation: Cell proliferation assays (Figure 5A,B,D,E) demonstrate significantly reduced growth rates in Pcgf6-KO ESCs and epiLCs, with growth arrest and cell death observed upon Pcgf6 deletion at ESC and epiLC stages. Phase-contrast microscopy (Figure 5A) shows that Pcgf6-KO ESCs maintain ESC-like morphology despite growth defects, distinguishing the phenotype from Max-KO ESCs.

results.result: PCGF6-PRC1-mediated gene silencing is essential for maintaining ESCs and epiLCs but not PGCLCs, with the same genes de-repressed across all three cell types.
results.evaluation: RNA-seq data (Figure 5G) show that the same PCGF6+RING1B+ genes are de-repressed to similar extents in ESCs, epiLCs, and PGCLCs upon Pcgf6 deletion. However, only ESCs and epiLCs exhibit growth defects (Figure 5D,E), while PGCLCs show accelerated differentiation (Figure 5F). This indicates that the phenotypic differences are not due to differential gene expression but rather to cell-type-specific requirements for PCGF6-mediated repression.

results.result: PCGF6 plays essential roles in pre- and peri-implantation mouse embryonic development, with Pcgf6-/- mice showing non-Mendelian ratios, embryonic lethality, and failure to establish ESC lines from knockout blastocysts.
results.evaluation: Genotype distribution data (Figure 6D) demonstrate significant deviation from Mendelian ratios at multiple developmental stages, with lethality detectable as early as 3.5 dpc. Embryo images (Figure 6E) show growth retardation in surviving Pcgf6-/- embryos at 10.5 dpc. ESC derivation experiments (Figure 6F) reveal complete failure to establish ESC lines from Pcgf6-/- blastocysts (0/22 lines), indicating functional defects in the ICM.

results.result: Loss of Pcgf6 causes pleiotropic developmental defects including anterior axial transformations, aberrant Hoxb6 expression, and impaired placental development with reduced spongiotrophoblast and trophoblast giant cells.
results.evaluation: Skeletal analysis (Figure 6G,H) demonstrates anterior transformations of the vertebrae in Pcgf6-/- mice, while overexpression causes posterior transformations (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C,D). In situ hybridization (Figure 6I) shows aberrant Hoxb6 repression at the eighth pre-vertebra. Histological analysis (Figure 6J,K) reveals significant reduction in placental size and dramatic decreases in spongiotrophoblast and TGC numbers.

results.result: PCGF6-PRC1 recruits PRC2 and mediates H3K27me3 deposition at target genes, though PRC2 has limited impact on transcriptional repression of PCGF6 targets.
results.evaluation: Tethering experiments (Figure 3A) show that ectopic PCGF6 recruitment leads to sequential RING1B binding, H2AK119ub1, and PRC2/H3K27me3 deposition. ChIP-qPCR (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E) confirms H3K27me3 enrichment at PCGF6 targets that is reduced in Pcgf6-KO and Eed-KO ESCs. However, gene expression analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) shows only limited de-repression in Eed-KO ESCs, indicating that H3K27me3 is not the primary repressive mechanism.

results.result: MAX/MGA independently recruits both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 to target genes, suggesting parallel repressive mechanisms.
results.evaluation: ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 3E) show that L3MBTL2 binding to gene promoters is maintained in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, indicating PCGF6-independent recruitment. However, ChIP-qPCR in Max-KO ESCs (Figure 4D) demonstrates that both PCGF6 and L3MBTL2 binding require MAX, supporting a model where MAX/MGA recruits both factors independently to mediate parallel repressive pathways.

results.result: DNA motif recognition by MAX is essential for ESC maintenance through recruitment of PCGF6-PRC1, as demonstrated by rescue experiments with DNA-binding-deficient MAX mutants.
results.evaluation: Cell proliferation assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A) show that wild-type MAX rescues Max-KO ESC growth defects, while DNA-binding-deficient mutants (VD, Δb) fail to rescue. Co-IP data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B) demonstrate that mutant MAX proteins retain the ability to interact with PCGF6, RING1B, and L3MBTL2. ChIP-qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C,D) confirms that mutant MAX fails to bind target genes and recruit PCGF6, establishing that DNA binding is essential for function.

results.result: PCGF6 binds in close proximity to transcription start sites at genes with shorter, more methylated CpG islands compared to canonical PRC1 targets, with distinct roles for KDM2B.
results.evaluation: Heat map analysis (Figure 1G) shows that PCGF6 exhibits sharp binding peaks at TSSs, unlike the broader distribution of RING1B, CBX7, and H3K27me3. Analysis of CGI characteristics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E) demonstrates that PCGF6 targets have shorter and more methylated CGIs than CBX7 targets. ChIP-seq analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G) shows that KDM2B loss has opposite effects on PCGF6 vs. CBX7 targets, suggesting distinct recruitment mechanisms.

results.result: H3K27me3 is dispensable for PCGF6-PRC1 recruitment, and the H3K27me3-dependent pathway for recruiting canonical PRC1 is not active at PCGF6 targets.
results.evaluation: ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C) show that PCGF6 binding and H2AK119ub1 levels are unaffected in Eed-KO ESCs, while PCGF2 (a cPRC1 component) shows minimal binding at PCGF6 targets regardless of H3K27me3 status. This demonstrates that PCGF6-PRC1 recruitment is independent of H3K27me3 and that cPRC1 is not recruited to PCGF6 targets via the canonical H3K27me3-dependent pathway.

results.result: The L3MBTL2/G9A/GLP axis and CBX1/3 play marginal roles in PCGF6-mediated repression in ESCs.
results.evaluation: Heat map analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) shows no considerable changes in H3K9me2 levels at PCGF6 targets in Pcgf6-KO ESCs, contrasting with L3mbtl2-KO ESCs. Gene expression analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) shows no significant changes in PCGF6+CBX7-RING1B+ gene expression in Cbx1/3-dKO ESCs. These data indicate that while these factors are present in the complex, they are not essential for PCGF6-mediated repression.

results.result: Anterior transformations in Pcgf6-/- mice are suppressed by Pcgf2 mutation, suggesting antagonistic functions of PCGF6 and PCGF2 in axial patterning.
results.evaluation: Skeletal analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E,F) demonstrates that the anterior transformations observed in Pcgf6-/- mice are suppressed in Pcgf6-/-;Pcgf2-/- double mutants. This genetic interaction suggests that PCGF6 and PCGF2 have opposing effects on Hox gene regulation and axial specification, though the molecular mechanism requires further investigation.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on PcG-mediated gene silencing mechanisms, including the roles of PRC1, PRC2, canonical and non-canonical PRC1 complexes, and their recruitment mechanisms.
results.evaluation: These claims are supported by citations to established literature and represent accepted knowledge in the field. They provide necessary context for understanding the novel findings about PCGF6-PRC1 but do not constitute new results from this study.
